claims.source: Both current components increased with increasing extracellular stimulus intensity (from 20 to 50 V), consistent with recruitment of at least one electrically coupled MLI (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing stimulus intensity-dependent responses in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Direct stimulation of neighboring MLIs in the presence of 10 µM NBQX revealed that each time an outward current was detected, it was preceded by a detectable inward current (n = 17/17 stimulation sites from 13 cells).
claims.source: When looking at the mean of all responses for each stimulation intensity, we found that each time an outward current was detected, it was preceded by a detectable inward current (n = 17/17 stimulation sites from 13 cells).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 17 stimulation sites across 13 cells.

claims.claim: Gabazine did not affect coupling coefficients between basket cells.
claims.source: Summary plot of unidirectional coupling coefficients (CCs), showing that they are not significantly altered by gabazine addition (n = 16 cells from 8 BC pairs, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, p=0.08).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of paired recording data from 8 BC pairs shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The amplitudes of the inward and outward currents (or their corresponding synaptic potentials) correlated with the bidirectional coupling coefficients for each cell pair.
claims.source: Indeed, the amplitudes of the inward and outward currents (or their corresponding synaptic potentials) correlated with the bidirectional CCs for each cell pair (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: Spikelets could generally be detected if the coupling coefficients were greater than 2%.
claims.source: Given the number of trials (n = 30 sweeps), spikelets could generally be detected if the CCs were greater than 2% (see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of detection thresholds shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The peak amplitude of the inward and outward currents, as well as the charge transfer of the spikelet response, were unaffected by altering the holding potential of the receiving neuron (n = 12 cells from six pairs).
claims.source: The peak amplitude of the inward and outward currents, as well as the charge transfer of the spikelet response, were unaffected by altering the holding potential of the receiving neuron (Figure 5B, n = 12 cells from six pairs).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 cells across 6 pairs shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: When adjusting the holding current to alter the membrane potential of the presynaptic neuron between approximately −80, –70 or −60 mV, the inward current component of the spikelet reduced in amplitude and the outward current component increased (n = 12 cells from six pairs).
claims.source: In contrast, when adjusting the holding current to alter the membrane potential of the presynaptic neuron between approximately −80, –70 or −60 mV, the inward current component of the spikelet reduced in amplitude and the outward current component increased (Figure 5D; n = 12 cells from six pairs).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 cells across 6 pairs shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The compound effect of inward and outward current changes led to an inversion of charge transfer from net excitation to net inhibition as the presynaptic neuron was depolarized.
claims.source: Because of the slower outward component, the compound effect of inward and outward current changes led to an inversion of charge transfer from net excitation to net inhibition as the presynaptic neuron was depolarized.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of changes in inward and outward currents with presynaptic membrane potential.

claims.claim: The slopes of the regression lines from the three presynaptic membrane potential groups (−60, –70 and −80 mV) were significantly different (F-test, p-value=0.0003), indicating that the ratio of inward and outward currents is a reliable indicator of presynaptic resting membrane potential.
claims.source: In paired recordings, the slopes of the regression lines from the three presynaptic membrane potential groups (−60,–70 and −80 mV) were significantly different (F-test, p-value=0.0003), indicating that the ratio of inward and outward currents is a reliable indicator of presynaptic resting membrane potential.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of regression lines from paired recordings.

claims.claim: The regression line of the off-beam stimulation group was comparable to the −60 mV group from paired recordings (p-value=0.93).
claims.source: The regression line of the off-beam stimulation group was comparable to the −60 mV group from paired recordings (p-value=0.93), but the linear relationship was significantly different from the direct stimulation group and the −60 mV group (p-value=0.01).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of regression lines.

claims.claim: MLIs in brain slices have a depolarized resting membrane potential, greater than −60 mV.
claims.source: Provided that the voltage-dependence of the shape of the presynaptic AP is similar between patch-dialyzed and unperturbed cells, these data indicate that MLIs in brain slices have a depolarized resting membrane potential, greater than −60 mV (i.e. more depolarized).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of spikelet waveforms between paired recordings and extracellular stimulation.

claims.claim: The depolarized membrane potential amplifies the AHP in the presynaptic neuron and ensures that spikelets deliver a net inhibition.
claims.source: This depolarized membrane potential amplifies the AHP in the presynaptic neuron and ensures that spikelets deliver a net inhibition, which provides another mechanism of FFI within the MLI network, in addition to chemical transmission.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of spikelet polarity dependence on presynaptic membrane potential.

claims.claim: Bidirectional spikelet transmission was significantly more likely to be observed than unidirectional GABAergic connections (58 ± 6%, n = 35/60 paired recordings, and 41 ± 5%, n = 35/85 connections, respectively; p=0.04).
claims.source: We found that bidirectional spikelet transmission was significantly more likely to be observed than unidirectional GABAergic connections, (58 ± 6%, n = 35/60 paired recordings, and 41 ± 5%, n = 35/85 connections, respectively; p=0.04, unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of paired recording data comparing electrical and chemical connections.

claims.claim: In 15 of 28 unidirectional connections from BC-BC pairs, the GABAAR antagonist gabazine did not alter the outward current amplitude.
claims.source: If we analyzed the gabazine experiments only, we found that in 15 of 28 unidirectional connections from BC-BC pairs, the GABAAR antagonist did not alter the outward current amplitude, consistent with a larger fraction of electrical than chemical connections.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data from 28 connections.

claims.claim: In the remaining connections where gabazine was tested, the fractional block by 10 μM gabazine was ~50% on average.
claims.source: In the remaining connections the fractional block by 10 μM gabazine was ~50% on average (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that, when both chemical and electrical synapses were present, the outward current under our recording conditions was similar.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: For cases where increasing stimulation intensity elicited a detectable outward current, the half-width in current-clamp conditions was decreased by 21 ± 4% (n = 9, p=0.004).
claims.source: For the cases where additional stimulation intensity elicited a detectable outward current, the half-width in current-clamp conditions was decreased by 21 ± 4% (n = 9, p=0.004; Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 9 stimulation sites shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Temporal summation of EPSPs in response to five stimuli at 50 Hz was significantly reduced at stimulus locations that recruited spikelets (n = 27 stimulation sites in the 'no spikelet' group versus n = 22 stimulation sites in the 'spikelet' group; p=0.004).
claims.source: Temporal summation of EPSPs in response to five stimuli at 50 Hz was significantly reduced at stimulus locations that recruited spikelets (Figure 7F; n = 27 stimulation sites in the 'no spikelet' group versus n = 22 stimulation sites in the 'spikelet' group; p=0.004, Two-way repeated measures ANOVA).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of temporal summation data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Coincident stimulation of spikelets and EPSPs increased the EPSP peak amplitude (averaged over a 4–6 ms window) by 21.3 ± 2.4% (n = 12, p<0.0001).
claims.source: Coincident stimulation of spikelets and EPSPs indeed increased the EPSP peak amplitude (averaged over a 4–6 ms window) by 21.3 ± 2.4% (n = 12, p<0.0001, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test - Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 cells shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: If spikelet recruitment preceded the EPSP (by 5 to 75 ms), the peak amplitude of the EPSP was significantly reduced, with a maximal reduction of 20 ± 2.9% at Δt = 20 ms (n = 12, p<0.0001).
claims.source: However, if spikelet recruitment preceded the EPSP (by 5 to 75 ms), the peak amplitude of the EPSP was significantly reduced, with a maximal reduction of 20 ± 2.9% at Δt = 20 ms (n = 12, p<0.0001, Wilcoxon matched-pairs; Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 12 cells shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: Spikelets concomitant with EPSPs reduced their half-width by 16.7 ± 1.8%.
claims.source: We also confirmed that spikelets concomitant with EPSPs reduced their half-width by 16.7 ± 1.8%, consistent with results described above in Figure 7D.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data consistent with previous findings.

claims.claim: The relative spike probability was increased by 49.3 ± 8% for coincidental arrival of both inputs, and decreased by 40.5 ± 6.1% if EPSPs were triggered 20 ms after the spikelets (p-values<0.001; n = 11 cells for both).
claims.source: We found that the relative spike probability was increased by 49.3 ± 8% for coincidental arrival of both inputs, and decreased by 40.5 ± 6.1% if EPSPs were triggered 20 ms after the spikelets (p-values<0.001; n = 11 cells for both; Wilcoxon matched-pairs; Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 11 cells shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: MLIs within the cerebellar cortex have been shown to provide feed-forward inhibition onto Purkinje cells in vitro.
claims.source: MLIs within the cerebellar cortex have been shown to provide FFI onto PCs in vitro (Dizon and Khodakhah, 2011; Mittmann et al., 2005; Valera et al., 2016) and in vivo (Arlt and Häusser, 2020; Blot et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: MLIs of the cerebellar cortex are known to communicate through both chemical and electrical synapses.
claims.source: MLIs of the cerebellar cortex are known to communicate through both chemical and electrical synapses (Kondo and Marty, 1998; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999; Rieubland et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: GABAergic chemical synapses provide self-inhibition between MLIs.
claims.source: GABAergic chemical synapses provide self-inhibition between MLIs (Mittmann et al., 2005), and have been suggested to mediate disinhibition of PCs (Blot et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Electrical synapses between molecular layer interneurons within the cerebellum have been shown to mediate synchronized firing.
claims.source: Electrical synapses between molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) within the cerebellum have been shown to mediate synchronized firing (Gaffield and Christie, 2017; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999) and sequence detection (Alcami, 2018), while those between Golgi cells have been shown to either synchronize or desynchronize cerebellar cortical network activity (Dugué et al., 2009; van Welie et al., 2016; Vervaeke et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The presence of electrical synapses has been shown to modulate passive properties in interneurons.
claims.source: Finally, the presence of electrical synapses has been shown to modulate passive properties in interneurons (Alcami, 2018; Amsalem et al., 2016; Hjorth et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Basket cells have been shown to precisely control the timing of Purkinje cell activity with millisecond precision.
claims.source: Specifically, basket cells (BCs) have been shown to precisely control the timing of PC activity with millisecond precision (Arlt and Häusser, 2020; Blot et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: MLIs in young animals have been shown to be electrically coupled via the gap junction protein Cx36, likely located in the dendrites.
claims.source: MLIs in young animals have also been shown to be electrically coupled via the gap junction protein Cx36, likely located in the dendrites (Alcami and Marty, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: There is an increasing spatial gradient of occurrence and strength of electrical connectivity between MLIs from increasing depths in molecular layer.
claims.source: It has been shown that there is an increasing spatial gradient of occurrence and strength of electrical connectivity between MLIs from increasing depths in molecular layer (Rieubland et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: MLIs located in the deepest (inner) third of the molecular layer are likely to be basket cells.
claims.source: Since MLIs located in the deepest (inner) third of the molecular layer are likely to be BCs (Sultan and Bower, 1998), we investigated if electrical transmission could be recruited in a feed-forward (FF) manner in the BC population, and how it modulates EPSP-spike coupling.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Spikelet transmission through electrical synapses has been shown to exhibit a long-lasting inhibitory current.
claims.source: Spikelet transmission through electrical synapses has been shown to exhibit a long-lasting inhibitory current (Alcami and Marty, 2013; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999; Rieubland et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Mefloquine is a potent blocker of gap junctions with approximately 70% block at 20 µM.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, 20 µM of mefloquine, a potent blocker of gap junctions (~70% block at 20 µM [Cruikshank et al., 2004]) reduced the frequency of observing an outward current to 14.9 ± 4.4%, with those detected currents being 3-fold smaller (8.7 ± 0.5 vs. 2.9 ± 0.3 pA; Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study characterizing mefloquine's blocking properties.

claims.claim: Previous reports showed complete block of electrical coupling at P10-13 in Cx36 KO mice.
claims.source: The remaining electrical coupling could be due to a late-onset (3–5 months) partial compensatory mechanism, in contrast to previous reports that showed complete block at P10-13 (Alcami and Marty, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The relative contribution of the depolarizing component or the after-hyperpolarization component of the presynaptic AP to the spikelet waveform can vary across cell types and determines if electrical synapses mediate net excitation or inhibition.
claims.source: The relative contribution of the depolarizing component (Hu and Agmon, 2015; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999) or the after-hyperpolarization component (Dugué et al., 2009; Vervaeke et al., 2010) of the presynaptic AP to the spikelet waveform can vary across cell types and determines if electrical synapses mediate net excitation or inhibition.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Alterations in the spikelet waveform can arise from alterations in presynaptic AP shape, which can be modulated by variations in the membrane potential of unperturbed neurons when they are not spiking (resting membrane potential).
claims.source: Alterations in the spikelet waveform can arise from alterations in presynaptic AP shape, which can be modulated by variations in the membrane potential of unperturbed neurons when they are not spiking (resting membrane potential) (Otsuka and Kawaguchi, 2013; Russo et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Theoretical studies show that net depolarizing spikelets will drive synchronization within neuronal networks, while hyperpolarizing spikelets will generate bistable networks which either oscillate synchronously or remain in asynchronous states.
claims.source: Theoretical studies show that net depolarizing spikelets will drive synchronization within neuronal networks, while hyperpolarizing spikelets will generate bistable networks which either oscillate synchronously or remain in asynchronous states (Ostojic et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a theoretical study.

claims.claim: Coherent firing of MLIs is required for encoding precise movement kinematics.
claims.source: Coherent firing of MLIs is required for encoding precise movement kinematics (Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Whisker movement kinematics can be both encoded and driven by precise PC firing patterns.
claims.source: Whisker movement kinematics can be both encoded (Chen et al., 2016) and driven by precise PC firing patterns (Bosman et al., 2010; Heiney et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Synchronized PC activity can precisely gate deep cerebellar nuclear neurons to drive movement.
claims.source: Synchronized PC activity can then precisely gate deep cerebellar nuclear neurons (Özcan et al., 2020; Person and Raman, 2012) to drive movement (Brown and Raman, 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In vivo evidence shows that BCs are involved in refining PC firing on the millisecond scale.
claims.source: Finally, in vivo evidence that BCs are involved in refining PC firing on the millisecond scale supports their important role in timing cerebellar cortical output (Arlt and Häusser, 2020; Blot et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Feed-forward inhibition supports rate-based modulation of excitation through gain modulation and increased dynamic range of the levels of excitatory input that can be encoded within a circuit.
claims.source: These different computational functions are classified according to canonical wiring motifs (Feldmeyer et al., 2018; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011): feed-back inhibition supports rate-based modulation of excitation through gain modulation and increased dynamic range of the levels of excitatory input that can be encoded within a circuit, while feed-forward (FF) inhibition permits precise regulation of postsynaptic spike-timing by sharpening excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)-spike coupling (Blot et al., 2016; Mittmann et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Feed-forward inhibition permits precise regulation of postsynaptic spike-timing by sharpening excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)-spike coupling.
claims.source: These different computational functions are classified according to canonical wiring motifs (Feldmeyer et al., 2018; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011): feed-back inhibition supports rate-based modulation of excitation through gain modulation and increased dynamic range of the levels of excitatory input that can be encoded within a circuit, while feed-forward (FF) inhibition permits precise regulation of postsynaptic spike-timing by sharpening excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)-spike coupling (Blot et al., 2016; Mittmann et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Feed-forward motifs can expand the dynamic range of inputs which can be represented by principal cells.
claims.source: FF motifs can also expand the dynamic range of inputs which can be represented by principal cells (Pouille et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Electrical synapses between neurons are thought to generate emergent properties such as oscillations and synchronized firing within neuronal assemblies.
claims.source: While chemical synapses can regulate interneuron firing in the same way as for principal neurons (Mittmann et al., 2005), the presence of gap junctions that couple neurons directly as resistive elements are thought to generate emergent properties such as oscillations and synchronized firing within neuronal assemblies (Beierlein et al., 2000; Bennett and Zukin, 2004; Draguhn et al., 1998; Gutierrez et al., 2013; Maex and De Schutter, 2007; Ostojic et al., 2009; van Welie et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Theoretical studies show the influence of electrical synapses in information processing within feed-forward circuits.
claims.source: However, despite theoretical studies showing the influence of electrical synapses in information processing within FF circuits (Pham and Haas, 2019), experimental evidence that electrical synapses modify temporally coded information within FF neural circuits has not been demonstrated.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a theoretical study.

claims.claim: Experimental evidence that electrical synapses modify temporally coded information within feed-forward neural circuits has not been demonstrated prior to this study.
claims.source: However, despite theoretical studies showing the influence of electrical synapses in information processing within FF circuits (Pham and Haas, 2019), experimental evidence that electrical synapses modify temporally coded information within FF neural circuits has not been demonstrated.
claims.evidence: The claim represents a gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claims.claim: Spikelet waveforms have been shown to depend on a variety of physiological parameters across different cell types, including resting membrane potential and active conductances in the presynaptic or the postsynaptic cell.
claims.source: Spikelet waveforms have been shown to depend on a variety of physiological parameters across different cell types, including resting membrane potential (Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999; Otsuka and Kawaguchi, 2013) and active conductances in the presynaptic (Curti and Pereda, 2004; Pereda et al., 2013; Russo et al., 2013) or the postsynaptic cell (Dugué et al., 2009; Mann-Metzer and Yarom, 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Previous recordings showing mostly depolarizing spikelets in cerebellar MLIs were due to either hyperpolarized holding potentials or an intrinsic difference in the amplitude of the AHP recorded from brain slices prepared from P11-13 rats.
claims.source: We postulate that previous recordings showing mostly depolarizing spikelets in cerebellar MLIs were due to either hyperpolarized holding potentials (Alcami, 2018) or an intrinsic difference in the amplitude of the AHP recorded from brain slices prepared from P11-13 rats.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors to explain differences with previous studies.

claims.claim: The resting membrane potential of MLIs is close to threshold.
claims.source: This robust recruitment can be accounted for by three factors: (1) overlap of MLI dendritic trees in order to more likely receive common synaptic input (see Figure 6A), (2) a resting membrane potential close to threshold (Figure 5E; Kim et al., 2014), and (3) a strong enough CC, sufficient to transmit detectable spikelets (>2.3%; Figure 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5E and citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The mean coupling coefficient between basket cells was 9.5%, similar to the 12% found in Golgi cells.
claims.source: The mean CC was 9.5%, similar to the 12% found in Golgi cells (Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to a previous study.

claims.claim: There is no correlation in coupling coefficient over intersomatic distances up to 60 µm.
claims.source: In support of the sagittal propagation of spikelets, we find no correlation in CC over intersomatic distances up to 60 µm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: In vitro experiments revealed that electrical connectivity in the MLI population increases convergence from MLIs to PCs.
claims.source: Moreover, in vitro experiments revealed that electrical connectivity in the MLI population increases convergence from MLIs to PCs (Kim et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The lateral spread of PF EPSPs through electrical synapses would contribute to increasing the effective convergence between MLI and PC.
claims.source: Finally, the lateral spread of PF EPSPs through electrical synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), as previously observed in Golgi cells (Vervaeke et al., 2012), along with spikelet transmission, would also contribute to increasing the effective convergence between MLI and PC.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations and comparison to previous findings.

claims.claim: A biphasic correlogram in vivo suggested an initial excitation of PCs followed by a brief (8 ms) inhibition of PC firing.
claims.source: In one of the few studies examining the activity of BCs and PCs in vivo (Blot et al., 2016), a biphasic correlogram suggested an initial excitation of PCs followed by a brief (8 ms) inhibition of PC firing.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Recent double-patch recordings in vivo show that even a single deep MLI (likely BC) can drive detectable inhibition of PC firing.
claims.source: Recent double-patch recordings in vivo show that even a single deep MLI (likely BC) can drive detectable inhibition of PC firing (Arlt and Häusser, 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: Voltage-clamp recordings in vivo showed that BC EPSCs are much faster than either SC or PC EPSCs in response to air puffs to the whisker pad.
claims.source: Interestingly, voltage-clamp recordings in vivo showed that BC EPSCs are much faster than either SC or PC EPSCs in response to air puffs to the whisker pad (Chu et al., 2012), consistent with the presence of electrical synapses, and perhaps explaining the predominant inhibition of PC firing in response to sensory stimuli (Bosman et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Millisecond inhibition of PC firing by sensory stimuli can disinhibit cerebellar nuclei, which in turn drive motor responses.
claims.source: Finally, in vivo evidence that BCs are involved in refining PC firing on the millisecond scale supports their important role in timing cerebellar cortical output (Arlt and Häusser, 2020; Blot et al., 2016). We therefore propose that eFFM could be an important mechanism to achieve robust, globally synchronous and precisely timed control of PC firing that in turn can efficiently drive cerebellar output from the deep nuclei.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and represents a proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: 60% of PF stimulus pipette locations within the BC dendritic tree at P30-60 produced sufficient excitatory drive in electrically coupled BC neighbors to reach threshold for APs.
claims.source: We observed that 60% of PF stimulus pipette locations within the BC dendritic tree at P30-60 (nearly 80% of locations in P90-150 animals – Figure 2) produced sufficient excitatory drive in electrically coupled BC neighbors to reach threshold for APs, and thus generate a spikelet in the postsynaptic cell.

claims.source: We observed that 60% of PF stimulus pipette locations within the BC dendritic tree at P30-60 (nearly 80% of locations in P90-150 animals – Figure 2) produced sufficient excitatory drive in electrically coupled BC neighbors to reach threshold for APs, and thus generate a spikelet in the postsynaptic cell.

claims.claim: This high degree of electrical connectivity can provide a global network mechanism spanning >100 µm in the sagittal plane for generating a feed-forward modulation of PC spiking patterns through synchronous inhibition.

claims.claim: Electrical feed-forward modulation could ensure an enhanced and brief BC network recruitment necessary for precise refinement of PC firing patterns.

claims.claim: Electrical synapses between BCs could provide a network-amplified, highly synchronous inhibition onto PCs along the parasagittal plane, despite complex spatio-temporal activation patterns of PFs.
claims.source: Electrical synapses between BCs could provide a network-amplified, highly synchronous inhibition onto PCs along the parasagittal plane, despite complex spatio-temporal activation patterns of PFs.

claims.claim: Spikelet transmission can propagate within the BC network to generate synchronous inhibition of Purkinje cells, which can entrain cerebellar output for driving temporally precise behaviors.
claims.source: Therefore, spikelet transmission can propagate within the BC network to generate synchronous inhibition of Purkinje cells, which can entrain cerebellar output for driving temporally precise behaviors.

claims.claim: Classical excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) are followed by GABAA receptor-independent outward currents, reflecting the hyperpolarization component of spikelets.
claims.source: By combining whole-cell patch-clamp and 2-photon laser scanning microscopy of basket cells (BCs), we found that classical excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) are followed by GABAA receptor-independent outward currents, reflecting the hyperpolarization component of spikelets (a synapse-evoked action potential passively propagating from electrically coupled neighbors).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental findings described in the abstract.

claims.claim: Feed-forward recruitment of the spikelet-mediated inhibition curtails the integration time window of concomitant excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) and dampens their temporal integration.
claims.source: FF recruitment of the spikelet-mediated inhibition curtails the integration time window of concomitant excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) and dampens their temporal integration.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental findings described in the abstract.

claims.claim: In contrast with GABAergic-mediated feed-forward inhibition, the depolarizing component of spikelets transiently increases the peak amplitude of EPSPs, and thus postsynaptic spiking probability.
claims.source: In contrast with GABAergic-mediated feed-forward inhibition, the depolarizing component of spikelets transiently increases the peak amplitude of EPSPs, and thus postsynaptic spiking probability.

results.result: Parallel fiber stimulation in basket cells produces GABAA receptor-independent outward currents that are mediated by gap junctions. These outward currents are detected in ~60% of stimulation locations, are blocked by NBQX, are insensitive to cesium replacement of potassium, are reduced by mefloquine and Cx36 knockout, and are independent of distance from soma.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9, C82-C85 provide converging evidence from pharmacological manipulations (NBQX, mefloquine, gabazine), genetic knockout (Cx36), ion substitution (Cs+ for K+), and spatial analysis. The data consistently support gap junction-mediated outward currents. Sample sizes are adequate (n=5-30 cells) and appropriate controls (DMSO, QX-314) are included.

results.result: Off-beam and direct extracellular stimulation of neighboring MLIs reliably evokes spikelet responses characterized by rapid inward currents followed by outward currents, with both components increasing with stimulus intensity.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 demonstrate that off-beam and direct stimulation consistently produce biphasic spikelet responses (n=11/11 and n=17/17 sites). The stimulus intensity-dependence (C11) and systematic presence of inward before outward currents support the spikelet interpretation. Claims C88-C90 acknowledge potential mixed responses but do not undermine the main finding.

results.result: Spikelet amplitude correlates with electrical coupling coefficient in paired BC recordings, with spikelets generally detectable when CC > 2%, and both are mediated by the same gap junctions.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15 show that gabazine does not affect CCs (n=8 pairs, p=0.08), spikelet amplitudes correlate with CCs, and detection threshold is ~2% CC. The correlation analysis and detection threshold determination are well-supported. Claim C91 acknowledges exceptions that may involve indirect coupling, and C92 provides a reasonable conclusion from the data.

results.result: Spikelet polarity is critically dependent on presynaptic but not postsynaptic membrane potential. Depolarization of the presynaptic neuron shifts spikelets from net excitatory to net inhibitory. Analysis of spikelet waveforms suggests MLIs have depolarized resting potentials (> -60 mV) in brain slices.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C22 provide systematic manipulation of pre- and postsynaptic membrane potentials (n=12 cells from 6 pairs) with appropriate statistical tests. The regression analysis (C19, p=0.0003) and comparison to extracellular stimulation (C20) support the inference about resting membrane potential (C21). The conclusion about net inhibition (C22) follows logically. Claims C93-C94 provide reasonable interpretations with appropriate caveats.

results.result: Electrical synapses between BCs are more frequent than GABAergic chemical synapses (58% vs 41%, p=0.04). When both are present, they contribute approximately equally to outward currents.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 shows statistical significance (p=0.04) but the comparison methodology is complex (bidirectional electrical vs unidirectional chemical connections). Claims C24-C25 provide supporting pharmacological data, but C96 acknowledges a significant limitation regarding potential rundown of GABAergic transmission that could bias the estimate. The conclusion (C97) is reasonable but the acknowledged limitation prevents full support.

results.result: Feed-forward recruitment of spikelets narrows EPSP half-width by 21±4% and dampens temporal summation of EPSPs at 50 Hz stimulation, similar to classical chemical feed-forward inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 provide clear experimental evidence with appropriate statistics (n=9, p=0.004 for half-width; n=27 vs 22 sites, p=0.004 for summation). Claims C98-C99 acknowledge potential confounds but C100-C101 provide reasonable conclusions. The experimental design comparing low vs high stimulation intensity is appropriate for isolating spikelet effects.

results.result: Coincident spikelet and EPSP stimulation increases EPSP peak amplitude by 21.3±2.4% and spike probability by 49.3±8%, while spikelet recruitment 20 ms before EPSPs reduces both. This represents a unique form of temporal contrast enhancement.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 provide strong experimental evidence from independent on-beam and off-beam stimulation (n=11-12 cells) with highly significant p-values (<0.0001). The timing-dependent bidirectional modulation is well-characterized. Claims C102-C104 provide appropriate interpretation of the temporal contrast enhancement mechanism. The experimental design effectively isolates spikelet effects from direct EPSPs.

results.result: Approximately 60-80% of PF stimulation locations recruit spikelets in electrically coupled BCs, due to overlapping dendritic trees, depolarized resting potentials near threshold, and strong coupling coefficients (mean 9.5%). This enables global network synchronization spanning >100 μm.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 document high recruitment probability with age-dependent increase. Claims C59-C61 provide supporting physiological parameters (resting potential, CC magnitude, spatial independence). Claims C113-C114 explain the mechanisms. Claims C74-C75 provide reasonable extrapolation to network function, though C75 includes speculative elements about functional consequences.

results.result: Electrical feed-forward modulation (eFFM) could provide network-amplified, synchronous inhibition of Purkinje cells to achieve precise temporal control of cerebellar output for driving temporally precise behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 and C105 propose mechanisms for how eFFM could function at the network level, but these are largely speculative extrapolations from the cellular data. Claims C106, C115-C116 acknowledge uncertainty with conditional language ('could'). While the cellular mechanisms are well-established, the proposed network-level and behavioral consequences require in vivo validation and are not directly demonstrated in this study.

results.result: The manuscript contextualizes findings within established knowledge about cerebellar MLI connectivity, feed-forward inhibition, electrical synapses, and motor control, while identifying a gap in experimental evidence for electrical synapse modulation of temporal coding in feed-forward circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C67 and C107-C118 appropriately cite previous literature to establish context. The citations appear accurate and relevant. Claim C56 correctly identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses. Claims C58 and C86 provide reasonable speculation about differences with prior work. These contextual claims support the novelty and significance of the current findings.

results.result: Experiments used appropriate methods including acute brain slices from P30-60 CB6F1 mice (both sexes), whole-cell patch-clamp with series resistance <30 MΩ, and liquid junction potential corrections.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 describe standard methodological details that are appropriate for the experiments. The age range, mouse strain, lack of sex bias, recording quality criteria, and junction potential corrections are all properly documented. These represent sound experimental practices.

results.result: The abstract summarizes that EPSCs are followed by GABAA receptor-independent outward currents (spikelets), which curtail EPSP integration but transiently increase EPSP peak amplitude and spiking probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 accurately summarize the main findings that are supported by the detailed results in the manuscript. These abstract claims are consistent with the experimental evidence presented in the full paper.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence (mefloquine block, Cx36 knockout) converge to support gap junctions as the mechanism for synapse-evoked outward currents.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 provides an appropriate synthesis of the pharmacological and genetic evidence. This conclusion is well-supported by the convergent experimental approaches.
